records.description: Flavor evolution can affect the interpretation of an astrophysical neutrino signal, but a source-to-detector prediction also needs the emitted flavor composition and spectrum, propagation environment and flavor-dependent detector response. A prescribed coherent trajectory Hamiltonian alone does not supply collisional, absorptive, self-refracting or expanding-universe transport. This graph admits the propagation implication and explicitly excludes quantitative astrophysical transport and cosmological predictions from this reconstruction.
records.name: Astrophysical and cosmological transport boundary
openObligations: The reviewed kinetic discussion distinguishes a normalized single-particle flavor density matrix from momentum-dependent occupation matrices. Emission, absorption, scattering and mode coupling require process kernels, occupation information and initial/boundary conditions; their normalization is not a universal trace-one probability. No collision coefficients, source spectrum, astrophysical flavor ratio or cosmological initial condition are supplied here.

The selected source describes cosmological expansion through momentum redshift and illustrates why collision integrals couple momentum modes. It does not justify obtaining a cosmological history by reusing a single vacuum L/E probability or a solar density profile. No expansion rate, decoupling prediction, abundance or mass constraint is inferred.

The bilinear Hamiltonian in Equation 2.5 explicitly leaves out neutrino-neutrino refraction. A self-consistent dense-neutrino medium would require additional interaction and angular/occupation inputs. The reviewed leading Liouville term also assumes slow phase-space variation; it is not an unrestricted exact kinetic solver.

Macroscopic phase averaging does not by itself establish environmental scattering, repeated collapse or a universal decoherence rate. Coherent forward matter effects, wave-packet overlap, unresolved-event averaging and collision-induced evolution are different mechanisms and retain their own conditions.

The present exclusions are finite limits of this admission, not a claim that such transport cannot be modeled. No new empirical acquisition, transport simulation, helicity-conversion model, universal thermalization theorem or source-detector fit is admitted.

records.name: Neutrino wave-packet overlap
openObligations: The approximation linearizes the dispersion relation over a narrow momentum distribution and neglects packet spreading. The characteristic length is shape-dependent, not an exact universal damping law or sharp boundary; equal group velocities produce no separation by this mechanism.

A source-only packet width is insufficient. A sufficiently coherent detection process can allow separated emitted components to interfere; the effective overlap already incorporates this condition, not an ordinary detector energy-bin width.

Loss of a local interference term does not establish fundamental nonunitarity, collapse, absorption or neutrino decay. Propagation through varying matter, scattering and environmental dynamics require separately specified evolution and are not derived here.

limitations: The measured beam observable is a proton-producing decay rate relative to the monitored neutron population in the trapping region. Identifying its inverse with the total free-neutron lifetime requires the stated decay-channel and detection assumptions. Storage disappearance and proton counting are distinct observables; no branching fraction or explanation of their difference is inferred here.

Nico 2005 refines the earlier report of the June 2000-February 2001 acquisition. Yue 2013 applies a new monitor calibration completed in 2011 to that same acquisition. These publications are not independent neutron-lifetime replications and cannot be averaged as such.

Cancellation of the neutron velocity distribution assumes a thin monitor with inverse-velocity response and unchanged beam between the trap and monitor. Finite absorption, spatial profiles, scattering and beam transport still require the original corrections.

The effective trap length is L=n*l+L_end. A fit of the proton-to-monitor count-rate ratio versus electrode number removes a constant end contribution only under the common-end-region assumption; the paper separately corrects nonlinearity from field, geometry and beam divergence. Proton trapping for milliseconds is not neutron storage for a lifetime.

The acquisition counts released decay protons in an accelerated silicon-detector readout and alpha/triton products from the downstream 6LiF monitor. Live time, timing-dependent backgrounds, dead time, proton backscatter, dead-layer loss and neutron corrections remain part of the analysis. The selected count files, geometry simulation and SRIM loss extrapolation are not independently replayed.

The published Nico 2005 result is 886.3+/-1.2 statistical +/-3.2 systematic seconds. The older preprint value is not substituted for this published result. Its absolute monitor calibration uses deposit characterization and an evaluated capture cross section; the old lifetime and that efficiency share calibration uncertainty.

The neutron-lifetime results do not establish neutron formation, proton stability, a universal constituent minimum or a present-day beam/bottle discrepancy. The 2013 historical world averages are not admitted without review of their components.

Nico 2005 refines the earlier report of the June 2000-February 2001 acquisition. Yue 2013 applies a new monitor calibration completed in 2011 to that same acquisition. These publications are not independent neutron-lifetime replications and cannot be averaged as such.

Cancellation of the neutron velocity distribution assumes a thin monitor with inverse-velocity response and unchanged beam between the trap and monitor. Finite absorption, spatial profiles, scattering and beam transport still require the original corrections.

The effective trap length is L=n*l+L_end. A fit of the proton-to-monitor count-rate ratio versus electrode number removes a constant end contribution only under the common-end-region assumption; the paper separately corrects nonlinearity from field, geometry and beam divergence. Proton trapping for milliseconds is not neutron storage for a lifetime.

The acquisition counts released decay protons in an accelerated silicon-detector readout and alpha/triton products from the downstream 6LiF monitor. Live time, timing-dependent backgrounds, dead time, proton backscatter, dead-layer loss and neutron corrections remain part of the analysis. studies.finding: The selected KRb singlet v=0 N=0 resonance shifts downward with applied dc field, while the N=2 response splits by angular-momentum projection. The zero-field N=0/N=2 interval is reported as 6.6836(5) GHz. These are spectroscopic frequency differences, before identifying a body-fixed moment through a rotational model. Ni et al. report B_Hz=1.1139(1) GHz and a body-fixed permanent-moment magnitude 0.566(17) D for 40K87Rb X1Sigma+ v=0, inferred from the N=0 Stark curve. The author thesis corrects the moment to 0.574(17) D after a plate-separation error. Use 1 D approximately 3.336e-30 C m. The N=2 curves test consistency within the same experiment.
limitations: The source preparation supplies molecules; the Stark response is not a universal molecular formation pathway or a bulk dielectric experiment.
The initial-state Stark contribution is neglected because the weakly bound starting molecules have a negligible moment in this treatment.
No direct charge-density image, force measurement, independently calibrated electric field or local spectral refit is supplied.

The result uncertainty is dominated by field calibration, not the statistical uncertainty of an isolated spectral line. Thesis Section 8.3 states 3%, while apparatus Section 3.2 estimates 3-5% and lacks independent field calibration; no reconciled error is invented.
The body-fixed moment does not imply a nonzero laboratory vector average at zero dc field. The thesis correction is not a new dataset or independent confirmation.

studies.finding: The published corrected acquisition gives 886.3+/-1.2 statistical +/-3.2 systematic seconds under the stated decay and detector assumptions.
limitations: The measured beam observable is a proton-producing decay rate relative to the monitored neutron population in the trapping region. Identifying its inverse with the total free-neutron lifetime requires the stated decay-channel and detection assumptions. Storage disappearance and proton counting are distinct observables; no branching fraction or explanation of their difference is inferred here.

Nico 2005 refines the earlier report of the June 2000-February 2001 acquisition. Yue 2013 applies a new monitor calibration completed in 2011 to that same acquisition. These publications are not independent neutron-lifetime replications and cannot be averaged as such.

Cancellation of the neutron velocity distribution assumes a thin monitor with inverse-velocity response and unchanged beam between the trap and monitor. Finite absorption, spatial profiles, scattering and beam transport still require the original corrections.

The effective trap length is L=n*l+L_end. A fit of the proton-to-monitor count-rate ratio versus electrode number removes a constant end contribution only under the common-end-region assumption; the paper separately corrects nonlinearity from field, geometry and beam divergence. Proton trapping for milliseconds is not neutron storage for a lifetime.

The acquisition counts released decay protons in an accelerated silicon-detector readout and alpha/triton products from the downstream 6LiF monitor. Live time, timing-dependent backgrounds, dead time, proton backscatter, dead-layer loss and neutron corrections remain part of the analysis. The selected count files, geometry simulation and SRIM loss extrapolation are not independently replayed.

The published Nico 2005 result is 886.3+/-1.2 statistical +/-3.2 systematic seconds. The older preprint value is not substituted for this published result. Its absolute monitor calibration uses deposit characterization and an evaluated capture cross section; the old lifetime and that efficiency share calibration uncertainty.

The neutron-lifetime results do not establish neutron formation, proton stability, a universal constituent minimum or a present-day beam/bottle discrepancy. The 2013 historical world averages are not admitted without review of their components.
